speechtext: Mr. ONBSIME GAGNON (Dorchester) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 132, to amend the Civil Service Act (Vacancies, outside service).

subtopic: EXCLUSION OP OUTSIDE SERVICE FROM OPERATION OP ACT
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: EXCLUSION OP OUTSIDE SERVICE FROM OPERATION OP ACT
speechtext:
The bill which I have the honour to sponsor speaks for itself; it needs no explanatory remarks. I feel, however, it is my duty to the house to say that I have studied the various questions involved, free from party prejudice and without the exaggerated zeal of a would-be reformer, but with a true desire to interpret the wishes of numerous people in Canada as well as of a great number of the members of this house, who contend that the Civil Service Act ought never to have been made to apply to the outside service, and that in the public interest reforms are urgently needed. Long before I had the honour of being a member of this house I had heard eloquent members of parliament denounce the Civil Service Act of 1919 as being inconsistent with the elementary principles of responsible government.
I have read the voluminous report of the Malcolm committee which was appointed by this house in 1923, and have studied the valuable recommendations made by the committee that wras appointed by the Senate in 1924. A good deal of evidence was adduced before the special committee appointed by this house in 1923. The deputy ministers' of

Civil Service-Outside Service
all departments appeared before the committee and made valuable suggestions. Amendments were contemplated, but no serious action has been taken. I venture to say that public sentiment in my province is strongly in favour of removing the outside service from the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Act. The people realize that the civil service commissioners, whatever may be their qualifications, cannot find the best possible candidates for all positions. It is indeed amazing to expect the same three men to find the best possible candidates for positions as varied, for instance, as a caretaker in the port of Vancouver, a customs agent in Gaspe, a director of expositions in London, England, and a postmaster in the district of the Yukon. It is amazing that the government of the day must rely entirely on these three men, who therefore must be practically encyclopedists of science to determine the qualifications required for such diversified positions.
As one may easily imagine, a great many mistakes have been made. The civil service commissioners cannot act alone. They have to ask for the assistance of employees of the departments, and in many instances appointments have been made by an employee of tbe department. On the other hand, the Civil Service Act prevents the ministers and deputy ministers from making appointments. The situation indeed is intolerable and ridiculous. This Civil Service Act subjects parliament to the authority of a kind of bureaucracy, which Lord Hewart of Bury, Lord Chief Justice of England, has happily called the New Despotism.
I might give instances to show that the operations of the civil service commissioners are frequently long drawn out and are therefore prejudicial to the best interests of the country. During the month of January notices wrere sent out throughout Canada that applications would be received to fill the position of director of expositions in London. Applications were sent in in the month of February. The examination was held on the first of May, and even yet, on the 20th of July, the director of expositions has not been appointed. During the month of March in Quebec city applications were called for the position of immigration inspector or guardian. Examinations were held in the months of April and May, and a report has not yet been made by the Civil Service Commission, and the Department of Immigration has therefore been obliged, pending a decision by the commissioners, to hire temporary inspectors, or guardians.
I need not go further to show that amendments to the act are necessary. As I said
before, in my humble judgment the time has come for a change. During the month of January I happened to express my views on this question in a public meeting, and immediately afterwards most of the newspapers of the city of Quebec, both French and English, and even the Montreal Gazette, approved of my humble views and stated that amendments ought to be made to the act, and that the somewhat kaiser-like powers of the commission ought to be at least curtailed. Being a new member I appreciated that I ought to avoid any hasty action, and therefore I consulted with a great number of eminent members on both sides of the house, as well as studied the valuable reports of the Malcolm committee and of the Senate committee. I realize, of course, that the Civil Service Act cannot be amended without the concurrence of both parties. The other day an interesting debate was held in this house, and I am very grateful to the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) for the views that he then expressed on this very question. May I ask you, Mr, Speaker, to give me leave to quote a few extracts from that speech, which really expresses the views shared by a great number of members on this side of the house. Mr. Chairman, I am
afraid I must make a few observations in respect to this matter. The Minister of

Saint John Harbour
Marine (Mr. Duranleau) was absent for two days when the matter became very pressing. A representative of Sir Alexander Gibb and partners visited Saint John harbour and made a report on conditions resulting from the disastrous fire which practically destroyed the whole of the terminal facilities. On the strength of his report it became apparent that the harbour commissioners would need a very much increased sum of money to enable them to carry on the repairs if the harbour facilities were to be made available for shipping by the first of December. But inasmuch as it would take weeks to prepare complete plans and specifications and call for tenders for the work as a completed unit, it was thought desirable to proceed at once with the necessary repair work. He asked the Foundation Company, the Northern Construction Company and J. W. Stewart Limited, and I think, one other company, if they would undertake the work on a cost plus basis, and they agreed to accept five per cent, which is a much lower charge than is usually asked for such work; but it was emergency work and they said they would undertake it for that figure. The work is being divided between them. It is not being taken out of the hands of the harbour commissioners, but inasmuch as the emergency was great, the department put its facilities behind those of the commissioners, and when it came down to the question of where an engineer could be secured who had knowledge of construction work, the experience of Mr. McDonald, of Halifax, was regarded as peculiarly fitting him for such work. I telegraphed him myself and asked him to meet the representative of the Gibb firm, which he did. The harbour commissioners of Halifax were asked if they would loan him to the harbour commissioners of Saint John for the purpose of directing the construction of the work which was to be undertaken to prepare the harbour facilities for use this winter. Very reluctantly they agreed to do so, and the harbour commissioners of Saint John are making arrangements to provide the harbour commissioners of Halifax with such engineering assistance as they may require during the absence of Mr. McDonald. Mr. McDonald who is a most experienced man in what you might term tidal water construction work, has gone over to Saint John and will stay with the undertaking until the work is completed. In the meantime the harbour commissioner's have not been in any sense supplanted, but with their cooperation the government is endeavouring to facilitate with all the rapidity possible completion of the work necessary 22110-250J
to make the harbour available for business this winter. Had any other method been pursued it is perfectly obvious that the work would not be done. I think it is only fair to say that the engineer of the Saint John harbour commission has sufficient work to do in connection with the general undertaking of engineering and also in connection with the new work that is being done in West Saint John, with respect to which the contract is outstanding and was outstanding when this government came into power. That work is being pushed forward to completion. I fancy it will not be completed for use this winter; in fact I know it will not, so the only facilities that can be relied upon will be berths 4 and 5 and 15 and 16 and a potato shed on 17 for the purpose of enabling business to be transacted as usual. The question of grain conveyors has been given a great deal of consideration and will involve an expenditure of half a million dollars, but unless there are legs on each of the docks it will be impossible, with the rapid tide, to move ships in a harbour like Saint John, and that work is being carried on. On pier 17, where the old potato shed was, a new shed will be erected to accommodate the requirements of shippers at that point.
I may add that there is no lack of harmony between the commission, the engineer whose services they have been fortunate enough to secure and the government in pushing forward the work. The $3,500,000 originally asked for by the harbour commission to complete what I might call the new work, together with the $1,500,000 bank loan will absorb $5,000,000, and leave substantially the same amount for the completion of the repairs in connection with the old facilities.

I wish to thank the right hon. Prime Minister for the full explanation he has given, which is perfectly satisfactory to me. The reports which have been appearing in the press left an impression such as the one I expressed this afternoon, and I wanted to have the matter cleared up. At the same time I wish to congratulate the government on accepting the estimate I gave the house following the fire. I then asked the government to vote $10,000,000, and that is the amount being provided.

Just a
word before the resolution is reported. I do not rise to delay the passage of the resolution; I think the government should be congratulated upon the speed with which they have attended to the situation existing in Saint John, but it is not with reference to that
Bonus on Wheat

matter I desire to speak. The Minister of Marine, in his preliminary remarks, and the Prime Minister in his more extended remarks, referred to a bank loan of SI,500,000. I think perhaps it would be well if the country had a little more information as to just how that loan was incurred. My understanding of the situation is that the previous harbour board let a contract to a concern known as the Atlas Construction Company for the building of what are termed the new works on the west side. That firm absolutely fell down on the undertaking, with the result that the people of this country have been called upon to pay a huge sum of money in excess of the contract price. I think these facts should be made clear.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Duranleau thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 134, to provide for a further loan to the Saint John harbour commissioners.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

On the orders of the day:

I should like to ask the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion) a question with reference to the Peace River outlet. I believe a conference was held the other day, and he may have something to tell the house with regard to this matter.

speechtext:
Yes, a conference was
held, but this is a large question and a great deal of consideration will be required before any definite statement can be given out. As soon as any real results come about I will be glad to tell my hon. friend and the house.
On the orders of the day:

I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion). There are several questions involved, in fact, but the answers are short and I believe the minister has the information before him. I should like to ask the minister: Is it true that the interest due on July 15 on the Toronto Suburban railway debenture stock has not been paid; are these debentures guaranteed by the national railways or by the government; what has been the financial situation of this railway with respect to earnings; how have interest payments been made heretofore; what action was taken by the national railways with respect to meeting the interest due on July 15 last, and what action will follow the said default in interest payments?

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman told

Three Rivers Harbour
my deputy this morning that he was going to ask some question in this regard, and I will give all the information I have. This is a matter entirely in the hands of the management of the road. The debenture stock is not guaranteed by the management of the national railways or by the government of Canada. This is a subsidiary of the national railways, but thei debenture stock is not guaranteed. I have been informed unofficially that the interest was not paid; I believe that to be correct, and I have no doubt it was a decision of the management-made because of the decreased earnings and lessened business of the Canadian National Railways.
In view of the fact that my hon. friend told my deputy he was going to ask these questions I obtained figures Showing the losses of this subsidiary. In 1930 the total deficit, including interest, amounted to $198,807, with an operating deficit of $77,000. In the previous year the operating deficit was $83,000, so I presume the management decided to withhold interest payments due to the depression, just as the dividends of various kinds of industrial corporations have been discontinued.
What would be the result of this electric railway falling back into the hands of the debenture owners?
I was told by the management some time ago that if they did default, every facility would be given the debenture owners, without expenses, to take possession.

Hon. ALFRED DURANLEAU (Minister of Marine) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to authorize a loan to the Three Rivers harbour commissioners not exceeding $700,000 for the construction of terminal facilities, upon approval by the governor in council of detailed plans, specification and estimates for such work, and the deposit of the debentures of the corporation to cover said loan.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. MacDonald (Cape Breton) in the chair.

What works will be
undertaken under this loan?	.

On September 18,
1929, an order in council was passed approving of the awarding of a contract to the Northern Construction Company Limited and
Three Rivers Harbour

G. W. Stewart for the amount of $2,660,535, for improvements in Three Rivers harbour. This was the lowest tender by $166,000, and according to the terms of the contract the works were supposed to be completed by October 31, 1931. Under a loan granted by this house the sum of $1,800,000 only was available. The contractors to date have carried out works amounting to $1,600,000, having ordered further materials amounting to over $200,000 to complete the contract. The works have progressed, but in such a way that the piers are not ready for use. The contractors have built the foundations of the whole work on which they have expended practically $1,800,000, but no section of it is yet completed. The whole of the loan made by this house of $1,800,000 has been expended to date, but, as I say, not a foot of these facilities is yet ready for use. We have to complete these works; there is no doubt about that; but we have tried as far as possible to save money. We have made some change in the plans resulting in a saving of about $300,000. Under the old plans, taking into account the small extras that have been provided for and the interest incurred during construction, together with engineers' fees and so on, we should have to ask the house for about $1,000,000 to finish the contract.
And the minister expects that with this $700,000 the work will be completed and will be available for use?

Yes; according to the reports of the chief engineer this amount will complete the undertaking. We found that, under the old plans, the pier, with two berths, was only 200 feet wide, and any practical construction man will realize that this is absolutely inadequate. Instead of building a 200 foot pier we have changed the plans somewhat, to make a straight line with the front of the government pier. This will provide a pier of 540 feet, with a 540 foot berth. The work will provide employment, because there will be a large amount of filling to be done, and we expect to have the filling made by the workmen of Three Rivers, as was done last winter. At that time, instead of securing the filling from dredging material, we provided work for the population of Three Rivers by getting earth from outside the city. It cost a little more than the sum charged by the contracting company, but under the circumstances we thought it wise to take that course in order to relieve unemployment.

My hon. friend knows
that, anything that will give work to the unemployed of Three Rivers meets with my hearty approval. Any information which I may desire I shall ask for when the bill is in committee.

I take it that the work
will be done under the 1919 Fair Wages Act, and that fair wages will be paid the labourers.

That is a matter to
be adjusted with the contractors.

I do not think the minister quite understands me. An act of parliament was passed in 1930, providing that all Dominion works shall be carried on under a fair wage clause, whether they are done by contractors or by the Dominion government itself, and I am asking the minister whether or not this work will be done under that law.

So far as I know,
the present government has not departed from the law mentioned by my hon. friend, and I do not think it will in this instance. These works are under contract and I presume there is in the contract a clause whereby the contractor will have to comply with the law regarding fair wages. This contract was awarded in September, 1929, by the former government, and presumably a fair wage clause was inserted. We do not intend to make an}'' change in the contract in that respect.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Duranleau thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 135, to provide for a further loan to the Three Rivers Harbour Commissioners.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Hon. E. B. RYCKMAN (Minister of National Revenue) moved the second reading of Bill No. 39, to amend the Customs Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. MacDonald (Cape Breton) in the chair.
On section 1-Discounts.
Will the minister explain?

I may say that this bill relates to nothing but administration, and it seems to me there can be difference of opinion with respect to only one matter which I had

Customs Act
better explain now. The act as it stands provides for certain penalties. To put the matter shortly, there is a maximum penalty of $500 and a maximum term of imprisonment of seven years. The situation is that the penalty of $500 is not sufficient and the term of seven years is too much. The fine of $500 is not sufficient because more in value can be smuggled so that it would pay a smuggler to have a maximum penalty of this amount. We seek to have that penalty made $1,000 The reverse is the case in connection with the term of imprisonment. The statute now provides seven years as the maximum, and that is too much, because juries will not convict and the accused is enabled to have twelve peremptory challenges instead of four. Since the maximum of seven years has been on the statute book there has not been one sentence of that term. We are anxious therefore that the term shall be reduced to four years and the statute made workable so far as the penalties are concerned. This question has given us a good deal of concern. It seems strange to increase the penalty in one case and to decrease it in the other. This in my opinion is the only point on which there would be any real difference, and I commend it to the committee.

Section 1, subsection 6
reads:
In estimating the value for duty no discount or deduction shall be allowed which is not shown and allowed and deducted-
The two last words are underlined.
-on invoices covering sales for home consumption in the country of export in the usual and ordinary course of trade.
Where discounts are actually allowed in the country of export, will they be recognized by our department and allowed in Canada?

The reason for the
addition of the words "and deducted" is that we want the invoices to show the true history of the sale. One would think if the discount were shown and allowed, it would hardly be necessary to have this provision that it be deducted. We want the discount to appear on the invoice as deducted, so that there is a written record of the transaction and it will not be necessary therefore to find out whether it has really been allowed or not. It is suggested for the purpose of enabling the importer to receive better terms. All that this means is that the honest transaction should stand and be shown completely upon the invoice.

That does not answer my
question which was this: If a United States manufacturer is allowing discounts to his customers in that country and he proposes to allow the same discount to his customers in Canada, will those discounts be recognized by the department?
They will be if the true history of the transaction as stated by my hon. friend is shown upon the invoice; if it is not a case of dumping, or if it is not a special rate fixed for duty.

There are
two provisos: the dumping and the special rate. There is no complaint about the dumping clause, but the department now have authority to fix value and under the circumstances I do not think this clause would be frequently applied.

The fixing of value does not arise in this case, but the hon. member for Weyburn put an all-embracing question that would include dumping duty and would mean, if a special value for duty purposes were fixed, and if the invoice showed what he stated, then we would be obliged to rely upon the invoice. But such is not the case. As I have stated, the intention is to have on the invoice, the actual, honest transaction or contract that the United States seller offers to the Canadian importer.

The other day when we
were discussing the items of the budget I made the statement that under our Customs Act and customs regulations as they now stand there is a temptation for a man importing grtods into this country from another country to pay a higher price to the foreign manufacturer than he need pay in order to escape the dumping duty. I said that our regulations permit him to do that and say to him:	If you actually do pay a higher price
to the foreign manufacturer you do not have to pay the dumping duty, but if you do not pay that higher price you will have to pav the dumping duty. When I made that statement the Prime Minister replied that that was not the case to-day, and I asked when it ceased to be the case, and he replied "Some time ago." I propose to prove not only that it can happen to-day but that it does happen, and not only that it does happen but that it cannot help but happen, just as I said.
I have here a letter from the Edgerton Manufacturing Company, Plymouth, Indiana,
Customs Act

dated March 17, 1931, of which I shall read
an extract:
You may be interested in knowing that the freight rate on the cars we shipped you during the 1930 season averaged 17-6 cents per dozen packages. This amount added to the price of $1.80 per dozen, as fixed by the Dominion government, would result in a cost to you of $1-976 per dozen without taking into consideration the duty. The action of the Dominion government would increase your delivered price approximately 25 cents a dozen and likewise would result in a profit to us of about 20 cents per dozen higher than that which we enjoy on sales made in the states. We feel that our profit on Canadian business should be approximately the same as that received in connection with business done in the states.
Yours very truly,
Richard W. Burg,
Traffic Manager.
I have another letter here from the Western Cartridge Company, East Alton, Illinois, dated May 6, 1930, a portion of which I shall read:
On January 3rd this year we reduced ammunition prices to all of our customers in the United States by 10 per cent, and we extended the same discount at the same time to our customers in Canada.
That is why I asked the question I did a minute ago. The letter continues:
The Canadian commissioner of customs has refused to accept this extra discount of 10 per cent on shipments of our goods into Canada, and has threatened to charge dumping duty against our goods so invoiced; and, based on this decision of the commissioner, we have been obliged to withdraw these reduced prices from our Canadian customers and are now invoicing them at a price 10 per cent higher than we charge any of our domestic jobbing trade. This additional 10 per cent is, of course, in the last analysis paid by the consumer of Western ammunition in the Dominion, and we regard it is distinctly unfair to him and his interests.
We have been told that the commissioner's decision was based on a brief presented to the Dominion government in Ottawa by the Dominion Cartridge Company, in which brief they indicated their reasons for protesting the reduction in price of American-made ammunition. We should like to obtain a copy of this Dominion Cartridge Company brief as presented to the government, in order to be in a position to present, if advisable, our answer to it.
I put a question on the order paper some time ago asking for a copy of that brief, but it was denied me. Here we find our customs department saying to the Canadian purchasers of American ammunition: You must pay 10 per cent more for that ammunition than these manufacturers are willing to accept from their American customers and 10 per cent more than they are asking you for, or otherwise we will make you pay that extra 10 per cent into the Dominion treasury. That 
is just what I said the other day would happen.
Here is a letter dated Ottawa, March 22, 1931:
In reply to your inquiry as to the effect of the change in discount on imported automobiles, basing the former discount at 30 per cent and the present discount at 20 per cent, the list price of the car being $1,000, I have to advise you as follows:
$1,000 less 20 per cent equals $800; at 20 per cent equals $160 duty.
$800 plus $160 equals $960 duty paid value; at 5 per cent equals $48 excise tax.
$960 at 1 per cent equals $9.60 sales tax.- Total, $217.60.
The next statement is this:
$1,000 less 30 per cent equals $700; at 20 per cent equals $140 duty.
$700 plus $140 equals $840 duty paid value; at 5 per cent equals $42 excise tax.
$840 at 1 per cent equals $8.40 sales tax.- Total, $190.40.
Then mark this statement:
If the importer pays $800 for his car special duty will not be applicable. On the other hand, if fie purchases the car at $700 a special duty equal to $100 will be payable.
R. W. Breadner, Commissioner of Customs.
The statement I made the other day that our customs laws and regulations as they stand at present tempt, almost force, a Canadian importer to send a larger amount of money out of the country to American or other foreign manufacturers in payment for his goods is amply substantiated by these letters, one of which is signed by the commissioner of customs himself. Not only does that happen, but under the act as it stands it must happen.
In the short session last fall we amended the Customs Act. I have a copy here of the amendments, but I shall read only the one that applies to this particular case. Section 2 reads:
Section 37 of the said act is repealed, and the following is substituted therefor:-
37. In determining the fair market value for duty of goods imported into Canada, the prices of which are published or listed by the manufacturers or producers, or persons acting on their behalf, the governor in council may from time to time fix and determine a certain rate of discount which may be applied to such published or listed prices, and such published or listed prices, subject to the deduction of the amount of discount, according to such rate, shall be deemed and taken to be the fair market values of any such manufactures or productions respectively as are specified in such order in council.
That is to say, we gave the minister power to fix a certain rate of discount on goods sent here at list price, and the list price after subtracting that rate of discount shall be

Customs Act
the value of the goods for duty purposes. At the same session last September we amended the customs tariff, section 6. I will read the amendment:
In the case of articles exported to Canada of a class or kind made or produced in Canada, if the export or actual selling price to an importer in Canada is less than the fair market value of the same article when sold for home consumption in the usual and ordinary course in the country whence exported to Canada at the time of its exportation to Canada, or is less than the fair market value, or value for duty thereof as determined under the provisions of section 36 of the Customs Act, or is less than the fair market value thereof as fixed by the governor in council under the provisions of section 37 of the Customs Act, or is less than the value for duty thereof as determined by the minister under the provisions of paragraph (a) and (e) of section 41 of the Customs Act, or is less than the fair market value thereof as fixed by the minister under the provisions of section 43 of the Customs Act, there shall, in addition to the duties otherwise established, be levied, collected and paid on such article, on its importation into Canada, a special or dumping duty, equal to the difference between the said selling price of the article for export and the said fair market value thereof or value for duty thereof; and such special or dumping duty shall be levied, collected and paid on such article although it is not otherwise dutiable.
I have ifnderlined the parts that apply particularly to the question we have under consideration, of goods shipped in here at list price, subject to discount. I will read now the underlined parts by themselves:
In the case of articles exported to Canada of a class or kind made or produced in Canada, if the export or actual selling price to an importer in Canada ... .is less than the fair market value thereof as fixed by the governor in council under the provisions of section 37 of the Customs Act, .... there shall, in addition to the duties otherwise established, be levied, collected and paid on such article, on its importation into Canada, a special or dumping duty, equal to the difference between the said selling price of the article for export and the said fair market value thereof or value for duty thereof; and such special or dumping duty shall be levied, collected and paid on such article although it is not otherwise dutiable.
In other words, Mr. Chairman, by the amendments made last fall we gave the minister power to fix a certain discount on these listed goods wdiich had the effect of fixing a certain value for duty. The value for duty having been fixed, then we amended the customs tariff in such a way that that value for duty as fixed by the minister had to be the actual purchase price of the goods. Therefore, if any man imported those goods into Canada for less than the price fixed by the minister he was exposed to the imposition of a dumping duty. The only way he could expect to avoid that dumping duty was to pay the same
amount of money over to the American manufacturer instead of paying it into the treasury.
That is the position in which we find ourselves as a result of the insane desire which possessed this government last fall to shut out goods from other countries at no matter what cost; it did not matter to them what the effect would be on Canadian trade; it did not matter what the cost would be to Canadian purchasers. The whole thing is this:	The Canadian importer is faced with
a choice of one of two things, either he must pay a higher price to the American manufacturer for the articles he buys or the government will fine him an equal amount in dumping duties. That is a situation I have repeatedly drawm to the attention of the minister and I hope he will understand what it means. I hope that at this session before the house prorogues an amendment to the customs tariff will be brought in which will give Canadians the right to purchase goods in other markets as cheaply as the people in other countries can purchase them, and legislation which will not force Canadians to pay a higher price to American manufacturers for the goods they wish to buy.

Would the minister tell
us whether the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) has correctly interpreted the act?
I was going to ask that.

Mr. Chairman, this bill
does not deal with the merits, if I may so call them, which the hon. member for Weyburn discussed. It says that a discount to be allowed must be shown upon the invoice, and this will be true whether or not the minister has power to fix the value for duty. It prescribes the form of the invoiee used when importing goods into Canada.

Those remarks refer entirely and only to the bill before the house at the moment. I hope hon. members opposite who have been so ready and willing to cry " Carried, carried " will take note of the remarks of the hon. member for Weyburn regarding changes made last fall. I think the hon. member has correctly placed the facts before the house.

We know
about that.
But the people at home do not know it.

I think the minister is quite right when he says that the matter to which the hon. member for Weyburn has referred
Customs Act

has no direct connection with the matter before the committee, and I may say in passing that I am in agreement with the legislation contained in this particular clause. I rise however to seek information on the point raised by the hon. member for Weyburn. Possibly I am out of order, but I think it only fair to revert to those matters because there may be no other opportunity of doing so. A few days ago I asked a question similar to that asked by my hon. friend from Weyburn, namely whether the dumping duty would apply when a value was fixed arbitrarily on any commodity imported into Canada, and whether, if the importer did not actually pay the price which was fixed arbitrarily for duty purposes only, the dumping duty would then apply. At that time the Minister of Finance (Mr. Bennett) replied that it would not, but I think he was in error. If in fact he was mistaken I think a correction should be made before the committee. Perhaps the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ryckman) would answer yes or no to the question asked by my hon. friend from Weyburn. I believe unintentionally an incorreot reply was made by the Minister of Finance. In my opinion the dumping duty does apply, and I must say we have pretty good proof of it. It always did apply under the old clause which permitted the governor in council, through the Minister of National Revenue, to fix a price on natural products. When we fixed a price on natural products that price was taken as the basis for a dump. I think the same was done when the minister fixed a price of $1 a ton on soft coal. If that soft coal was actually purchased at 60 cents a ton, as it might have been, then the duty was 50 cents a ton. There was a dump however of the difference between 60 cents, the actual price, and the dollar fixed by the minister. I think then the dump of 40 cents was applied. If it was done in one case I suppose it would apply in all other cases, but I think the minister should say whether or not that is the fact.
Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend from North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) has admitted that this discussion is outside the ambit of the bill.
I asked the question only because a wrong answer was given.

The Prime Minister having given one answer and the hon. member for North Waterloo being of another opinion I should like to look into the matter before stating my view.
[Mr. EuJer.l
I feel the proper view is that expressed by the hon. member for Weyburn.
We ought to know what the minister thinks.
If the minister is not sure we shall have to ask him some other time.

If he is not sure, I think he ought to be, because three months have passed since I first drew his attention to the matter. The other day when I mentioned it again he laughed, and he laughs now. Surely he ought to have a serious moment when he might look into the matter. I think we have a right to know the correct interpretation of the law. There is a law which gives power to fix an arbitrary valuation, and which states that the difference .between the invoice price and the price he fixes shall be levied and paid.
I do not think the matter is debatable on this particular section.
This section deals with discounts.

The section now before the committee merely refers to the administration of the act and states that the words "and deducted" shall be added to the section. The minister says he will deal with the point raised by the hon. member.

Section agreed to.
Sections 2, 3 and 4 agreed to.
On section 5-Territorial waters defined.

Mr. Chairman I desire to move an amendment to this section. My reason is that recently there has been a decision of the Supreme Court of Canada which would show that the present section is ultra vires of this parliament. An appeal is being taken, but if the statute of Westminster comes into force this section 5 will be appropriate. I am therefore asking to make this amendment:
That subsection 7 of section 5 be amended by adding thereto the following:
Subsection 7 shall come into operation upon a date to be proclaimed by the governor in council and published in the Canada Gazette.
I will ask my hon. friend the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Rhodes) to move this amendment.

I move the amendment
accordingly.

Three or four years ago,
when I had the honour of being Minister of

Customs Act
National Revenue, I introduced an amendment which was carried under some protest, extending the ordinary three mile limit to twelve miles with regard to the right of seizing liquor-laden vessels which were supposed to be destined to Canadian ports. At that time I think the present Prime Minister and others questioned the validity of such an enactment. However, I said, "We will try it for what it is worth." The minister has now referred to the fact that in a case brought into court recently the section was declared ultra vires, and that the government proposed to lodge an appeal. I suppose that means that the case will be appealed to the privy council. If this section is acknowledged hy him to be ultra vires, is he hoping by an appeal to the privy council to establish the validity of the amendment made some years ago?

We hope to establish
the validity of this legislation and that the decision of the supreme court is wrong in law. We are supporting, as I understand it, the position that was taken by my hon. friend some years ago. The decision of the supreme court is to the effect that outside the three mile limit we have not the jurisdiction which my hon. friend desired to give, and which we desire to maintain.
I am very glad to hear that, for it rather vindicates the position I took at the time, and indicates a right-about-face on the part of those who then opposed it.
We are always just.

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 6-Arrest without vrarrant for indictable offence-jurisdiction of officer making arrest.

What is
the reason for the reference to the criminal code?

At present there may
be offences against the Customs act that would not be indictable under the criminal code. Naturally we want to have it declared by this legislation that indictable offences whether against the Customs act or the criminal code may be dealt with by customs officers acting on reasonable and probable grounds.

Does it not in effect mean
that where a regular customs officer has the right by virtue of his office to make an
arrest, and, the ordinary preventive officer has not that right, it is proposed to give the latter that right?
Yes.

I should like to know exactly what powers the minister gives to his preventive officers. I received a complaint some time ago that a certain family on returning home found their house in possession of a stranger who had broken open a trunk and was rifling the contents. On being asked what business he had there he said he was a preventive officer and had a right to make the search. I should like to know from the minister whether if a man finds a stranger in his house under those circumstances he has not a right to use a club on him?

The facts to which my hon. friend refers have not come to my notice. In the past preventive officers have been men who have a reasonable knowledge of their duty and act accordingly. I can think of only two cases of the kind mentioned by my hon. friend. If there is an honest belief on the part of the preventive officer that the customs laws have been broken, for instance, that goods have been smuggled, then the officer has specific instructions to proceed just as if he was following His Majesty's writ and make a search. I would be very much surprised to hear that officers of the preventive service were guilty of making oppressive searches without being properly instructed and without a reasonable belief that the law had been infringed.

Who gives them the
necessary authority?

The officers have the
authority that the statute gives them. There is a chief inspector and I have no doubt that any preventive officer would consult the chief inspector before making an oppressive search, unless he was in the very midst of infractions of the customs law. There are no officers running around loose jumping into men's houses and ransacking them. As I say, I have heard of only two cases of the kind mentioned by my hon. friend from Weyburn (Mr. Young). In one of those cases there was absolute justification; as to the other case I have not yet heard all the facts.

I think it might be correct
to say that their powers of search come under a writ of assistance granted by the Exchequer Court of Canada.

Section agreed to.

On section 9-Further penalty if value two hundred dollars or over.

I do not understand from
the explanatory note the reason for the reduction of the minimum fine from $500 to $200. I am not objecting to it particularly, but I should like to know the reason for the change.

As the note explains,
the maximum fine, not the minimum, was $500. We desire now that the maximum fine be $1,000 and the minimum $200. Formerly the term of imprisonment was seven years, now we desire that it be made four years for the reason stated in the note. There has not been one conviction under this seven year law and we feel there must be a stringent law that will compel the observance of the Customs Act. If hon. members will read the note they will see the purpose of the legislation.

In the explanatory note on the opposite page I find the following words:
-it will be made more difficult for a defendant by exercising his right of peremptory challenge to select a jury to his liking.
Is that the purpose of the legislation, to make it more difficult for the defendant?

No; my hon. friend does not understand it correctly. This will make it more difficult for the defendant to get a jury to his liking. When the term of imprisonment may be five years or over the accused is allowed twelve challenges; when it is under five years he has but four challenges, and we desire that the defendant should have but four challenges. In cases of this kind it is hard to get a jury who will find a man guilty when the penalty may 'be seven years imprisonment, no matter how serious the infraction of the law, but at one time-and my hon. friends know when that was-parliament thought it advisable to make the penalty seven years. That has not accomplished what parliament set up to do.

Section agreed to.
Sections 10 to 17 inclusive agreed to.
On section 18-Where goods of the value of two hundred dollars or over.

I think this embodies a very radical departure from the old act. Perhaps I might refer to something that is more or less history. Three or four years ago, Shortly after the customs investigation, it was thought desirable that persons who smuggled goods to the value of $200 or over, if found guilty should be sent to prison without the option of a fine. I remember that when I introduced the amendment I found a great deal of

opposition from those who were supposed to be supporting me and a great deal of support from those on the opposite side, I think notably the present Prime Minister, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Justice. That amendment was adopted. Now I see there is a departure from that method; I take it that this clause means that a person convicted of smuggling to the value of $200 or over need not necessarily be sent to prison but that the judge has the option of imposing a fine or imprisonment. I should like to ask the minister if that is not the meaning of this section.
That is quite correct.

I think the reason for this change is that in some of the provinces east of Ottawa-we will not say just how far east- it was found impossible to get a conviction in connection with liquor smugglers who had brought in good's to the value of $200 or over, so that really the law was a dead letter and defeated its own purpose. Juries would find culprits not guilty rather than find them guilty and send them to gaol. Perhaps they would have been quite content to bring in a verdict of guilty if a substantial fine could have been imposed. I am rather inclined to agree with this change; in fact last year I had some thought of bringing in an amendment to the same effect, but I was just a little doubtful whether one should make a right about face so quickly. I am quite in accord with the amendment now proposed.
I should like to ask how far back in a man's career the officials may go to get this total value of S200. Will they go back six months?
No, this means for one offence.

This is the way I have known it to work out: A certain man's house was raided and the preventive officers searched through his papers. He had been indiscreet enough to keep papers; he had kept all his store bills for years back. He lived near the border, a long distance from any Canadian town and had purchased goods in the United States because there was no other place where he could buy them. He had purchased lumber there which was incorporated in his buildings. The preventive officer came along and found these papers-

Showing he had bought
these goods in the United States. There was no place within miles where he could report them, after he had purchased them in the

United States because it was the handiest place, and in fact, the only place where he could buy them. He did just as you or I would have done.

from that statement.

I hope my hon. friend is

The preventive officers totalled up the bills, which ran into several hundred dollars and the poor fellow is billed with an amount he will never be able to pay as long as he lives. I want to ask the minister if there should not be a time limit in connection with these offences.

Does my hon. friend mean

Yes.
Mr. EULEiR:	Surely that would not be

On section 19-Officials with powers of two justices.

I should like to point
out that some farmers who live close to the boundary find great difficulty in locating a customs officer in order to report their purchases; in the sparsely settled districts they may have to travel thirty or forty miles. I know that the difficulty of which my hon. friend speaks does exist, particularly in districts such as the one from which my hon. friend comes, where there are stretches of land along the border perhaps
sparsely settled. There is difficulty experienced by a resident in passing his goods through customs, and endeavour has been made by the department to help in these cases, where that can be done reasonably. In some cases I understand they have been allowed to observe the customs law in a generous way, always keeping in mind the necessity for the collection of the full duty. There is that difficulty, however, and if my hon. friend has anything to suggest I will be glad to consider it.

I do not see why the mounted police or some other authority could not take from settlers a list of their effects and report to the customs. In my constituency there is one section in which the customs offices are some 60 or 70 miles apart. A man coming with a wagonful of settlers' effects and desiring to settle close to the line discovers when he gets there that he must go still further north into Saskatchewan, a distance of 30 miles, before he can find roads going east and west. He then has to travel east 40 miles and south a considerable distance, so that altogether he is put to a great deal of unnecessary trouble. It seems to me that he might go to a justice of the peace or some designated person of good repute who would take a statement from him as to the amount of goods he had brought in, exempt by reason of being settler's effects. I submit that some arrangement of that kind should be made.
Section agreed to.

I was not here when section 5 was passed, and I should like to ask the minister a question regarding it. On a former occasion I took the position that the power which the department sought in this regard was really ultra vires of parliament. subtopic: INCREASE IN PAYMENT TO PROVINCES FROM FIFTY TO SEVENTY-FIVE PER CENT

speechtext:
Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (for Mr. Bennett) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend the Old Age Pensions Act by increasing the amount of the payment to the provinces for old age pensions from one-half to seventy-five per cent of the net sum paid out during the preceding quarter by such province for pensions, and to provide for the examination and audit of expenditures in the province and the accounts relating thereto.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. MacDonald (Cape Breton) in the chair.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: INCREASE IN PAYMENT TO PROVINCES FROM FIFTY TO SEVENTY-FIVE PER CENT
speechtext:
It will be observed that the only
change is the substitution of "seventy-five" for "fifty," and to provide that the acceptance of the increased amount shall enable the Dominion to make such investigations and inquiries as may be necessary to ensure that the moneys so paid have been expended for the purposes intended. The statute provides that the agreements shall have a life of at least ten years. That is to say, the existing agreements are predicated upon the assumption that the provisions of the statute regarding the length of time during which the subsidy of fifty per ednt was payable shall be maintained for ten years. There may be some questions to be considered later in that regard, but at the moment no question arises with respect to the substitution of "seventy-five" for "fifty." My only regret is that the situation does not warrant making the sum larger. In any event the whole proposal is but temporary in character, and contemplates a contributory system to old age pensions as was mentioned in the House of Commons when the Old Age Pension bill was under consideration. For that reason this provision has been made for the year.

speechtext: Can my right hon. friend indicate what additional outlay will be occasioned per annum under this change?

speechtext: Of course it is exactly half as much again as we paid last year. A few days ago I gave the figures, but I do not care to rely upon my memory. I shall see that they are given.

speechtext:
The point I should like to make is that this means a very considerable increase in the amount of money to be handed over from the federal treasury

Old Age Pensions Act
to the provinces for their administration. The Prime Minister has, I think, indicated if not promised that the present administration will give 100 per cent of old age pensions, and if that is what he is working up to by this measure, it seems to me that the time already presents itself when he should consider the desirability of having the entire fund administered by the federal government. I cannot see any justification for the government handing hundreds of millions of dollars- because that is what this ere long will likely mean-over to the provinces for them to administer as an old age pension fund, the federal parliament providing something like 100 per cent of the oultay, and not itself taking in hand the work of administration. The constitutional difficulty was among the reasons why originally, when the Old Age Pension Act was passed, there was an arrangement whereby 50 per cent of the amount would be transferred to the provinces. But it was never contemplated that if .that amount of 50 per cent were exceeded, the federal government itself would not take over the administration of the old age pension law in its entirety. I should like to suggest to my right hon. friend if anything of this kind is in contemplation and the British North America Act in any respect stands in the way, he should take immediate steps to have the provisions of the act so amended as to give the federal government the right without delay to administer the entire old age pension law.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
The suggestion of the right hon. gentleman is a most reasonable one, but I think the ex-Minisiter of Justice will agree that when the statute of Westminster is passed we shall find it much easier than we do now to deal with a situation of this character. My own view is that no amendment to the British North America Act is required to deal with this problem on one phase of it, and in the preamble to the bill I have indicated that the census of the year will form the basis of actuarial computations that would warrant a contributory system on a national scale being embarked upon. As the right hon. gentleman will recall, we discussed that without going into detail when the original proposal was made. As the matter stands, I know of no constitutional impediment to the federal parliament voting 50 per cent of the sums paid by the provinces to old age pensions. I think it will be agreed that if there is no constitutional impediment against paying 50 per cent, there is none with respect to paying 75 per cent, and it is clear that it is not only probable but almost
certain that there will be an increase in the payments made under this statute by reason of other provinces, now that the sum has been increased to the amount I have mentioned, availing themselves of its provisions. In the meantime I assure the committee that the whole problem is being considered from the angle of a contributory system predicated upon an actuarial valuation of the liabilities that would be involved. That is not as simple as perhaps would appear from the mere statement of it, but this year's census will enable us to determine with some degree of exactitude what is involved, and if there are any constitutional limitations upon our activities in that direction, I think the house will be only too glad to remove them. I do not contemplate any difficulty on that score.

I understand

I would like to call the Prime Minister's attention to what appear to be to me one or two injustices in the working out of the present act. In one case a woman who has lived all her life in Canada, and raised a family here, now finds herself with her husband dead, her family scattered, and no home of her own in any province; she spends her time living with friends, a few months in Ontario, a few months in Manitoba, a few months in Saskatchewan, and so on. Yet she is totally unable to qualify for an old age pension because she cannot establish "residence in any province.
The other is the case of a woman who came to this country when she was over fifty years, who speaks a foreign language, and settled in a remote district where there was no opportunity to learn the English language.

I can only say in reply to my hon. friend from Weyfourn that whatever difficulties may have been experienced, this statute does not endeavour to remedy them; it merely accepts the situation, and increases the financial responsibility from 50 to 75 per cent. There have been what appeared to be cruel hardships in some cases, and there have also been impositions upon the fund in other cases. I would hesitate to take the time of the committee in indicating some of the charges on the fund which have been imposed upon the provinces, as well as upon the Dominion. People in moderately good circumstances have disposed of their properties and qualified to receive the old age pension. It dame to my attention that in one case there was quite a little settlement of them in one province receiving the $20 per month, and when one of them presented his cheque to the bank for payment, the

Old Age Pensions Act
banker said, "What is this for? Surely you are not getting an old age pension, because you have a substantial sum of money on deposit in this bank." The man said that he had managed to get it, that somebody had told him he should have it. It is cases such as that which impel the addition of a provision to provide for the closest scrutiny with respect to payments.

subtopic: INCREASE IN PAYMENT TO PROVINCES FROM FIFTY TO SEVENTY-FIVE PER CENT
speechtext: Should a contributory system be under discussion there may be differences of view with regard to it, and the government may be faced with the possibility of having to carry on the original scheme increasing to 100 per cent the amount that is going to the provinces, or take over the entire administration itself. I would therefore suggest that the Prime Minister institute steps immediately to clear the way for the possibility of the federal government itself at the earliest possible moment administering the old age pension scheme, so that if parliament is asked to make any larger contribution out of the federal treasury it will be sure that it will have the right to administer the moneys in its own hands, and that no exception can be taken to its administering the scheme in its entirety. Indeed it should secure this right where the amount of the federal contribution exceeds 50 per cent as will be the case when the bill based on this resolution is enacted. I suggest to the Prime Minister that he consider that aspect of it and secure as early as possible some amendment, to the British North America Act, if that be necessary, to enable the federal government from now on to administer the old age pension act.

subtopic: INCREASE IN PAYMENT TO PROVINCES FROM FIFTY TO SEVENTY-FIVE PER CENT
speechtext:
I am rather surprised that
the Prime Minister has announced what really is a very important departure of policy at this late stage, and in a rather casual way, connected with a bill that does not immediately refer to that matter. He must have had it somewhat in the forefront of his mind, for he tells us that he has been .consulting the actuaries of the department with regard to it. I cannot recall that it formed any issue on any platform in the election campaign, or that any reference was made to it in the speech from the throne, and it would be there that I would look to see what really is a radically new policy. The Prime Minister has indicated that he does not wish to discuss details, but perhaps he would oblige me on this one point. As has been pointed out, if contributions are made compulsory the question of constitutionality will arise. If, as the Prime Minister rather indicated, the contributions are
made voluntarily, then this question will arise:	Thrifty people, good citizens perhaps,
would make their contributions, but there is always a proportion who are not good citizens and who dissipate any money they get one way or another, and when they come to old age they would be old and destitute and yet would not be eligible for relief. Could we tell them: It is your own fault. You should have contributed to this voluntary scheme when you were young and able? To tell anyone in such circumstances that he or she should have done something years ago is very little use. It is our duty to let no one starve in this country. I have no doubt that the Prime Minister would be fully aware of that aspect. What I wanted to ask was, would the Prime Minister be willing to give the assurance that in case such a contributory scheme is started, those who are now old and unable to contribute will be taken care of under the present system or something allied to it.

subtopic: INCREASE IN PAYMENT TO PROVINCES FROM FIFTY TO SEVENTY-FIVE PER CENT
speechtext:
Before the Prime Minister
thinks of adopting any scheme of contributory old age pensions I hope he will give the matter his very serious consideration, because I know of no English-speaking country where a person receiving a pension at the age of seventy pays any contribution towards pension. In Great Britain, of which the Prime Minister spoke, the pension is paid at the age of sixty-five, and the pensioner contributes towards that pension only for that portion of his life between sixty-five and seventy years of age. Beyond seventy years of age the whole obligation becomes a national obligation and the pensioner contributes nothing. Consequently there is no analogy between the system of pensions in Great Britain and the system of pensions in this country. I am not going to speak on the constitutional side of this question. I know it is very important. I am afraid, however, that if we were to attempt a compulsory system of pensions on a contributory basis, it would be almost impossible in this Dominion.
My reason for rising was to speak about another matter which has not been mentioned this afternoon. It is one which I am sure will appeal to the sympathies of most of the members of the house. For a number of years there has been a very strong agitation in Canada to give pensions to the blind people of this Dominion, and I am just wondering if the government would take into consideration the question of providing pensions for the blind. I am not at the moment fully conversant with the provisions of other old age

Old Age Pensions Act

Pensions acts in other countries or how they deal with the blind, but I am under the impression that in some countries where the blind people receive a pension there is a special provision in the act whereby blind people are eligible for the pension at an age much below that of the ordinary pensioner under the act. I was wondering if the government would take into consideration, when the act comes before parliament this session, the insertion of a clause which would give to the blind people of this Dominion a pension at an age at which I think the blind people ought to receive it. I think the matter speaks for itself, and undoubtedly action will depend on possibilities of financing. Weyburn referred to some of the difficulties in connection with the administration of the act, and I pointed out that when the statute was passed in 1927 these words were inserted as section 4:
Every agreement made pursuant to this act shall continue in force so long as the provincial statute remains in operation or until after the expiration of ten years from the date upon which notice of an intention to determine the agreement is given by the governor general to the lieutenant governor of the province with which the same was made.
The act contemplated that in the first instance the provinces should pass old age

Old Age Pensions Act
pensions statutes, such matters being clearly within their constitutional rights. Then the Dominion undertook to pay 50 per cent of such expenditures. Section 5 further provides:
Before any agreement made pursuant to this act comes into operation the governor in council shall approve the scheme for the administration of pensions proposed to be adopted by the province, and no change in such scheme shall be made by the province without the consent of the governor in council.
In other words, by the joint operation of provincial and federal statutes the agreement becomes one which cannot be altered by either party without the consent of the other. For instance when the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River refers to difficulties connected with the five year period I point out to him only that the statute was in operation from 1927 until 1930, during which time no change was made, and it still remains as it was passed. Whether or not it was thought desirable to leave it as it is one can conclude only from the fact that it was not changed.
With respect to what has been said by the hon. members for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) and Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) concerning the blind, I may say that representations no doubt similar to those made to previous governments were made to the present government respecting these most deserving people. It is admitted that in the first instance the obligation is provincial in character. Until further provisions are made by the provinces it would be obviously unfair to ask the Dominion to carry the load, for the simple reason that for many years the education of the blind has engaged the attention of provincial legislatures. For instance in Nova iScotia, where I believe there is one blind person for every 1,000 of population, there is a school for the blind, the principal of which was honoured by His Majesty some years ago with a knighthood. The school has an international reputation, and through the expenditures by the province as well as private benefactions it has been enabled to carry on a very excellent work. I think the same may be said concerning other provinces. The federal government donates a small sum to two or three organizations in the province of Quebec which have in view the interests of the blind. Ontario makes the same provision as do the other provinces for the education of the blind. Concerning a pension for the blind, I spoke to the delegates of organizations which appeared before me in practically the same terms as did my predecessor, namely that in the first instance the provinces have not indicated any intention of taking action.
Until they do indicate a determination to discharge an obligation which constitutionally is theirs, action by the federal government will have to wait. Of course the blind who have been deprived of their sight by the war are taken care of by the military pensions act.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), for some reason best known to himself, said that in my remarks to-day I had proposed a policy. I did not do that, nor had I any intention of so doing. I said to him and to the committee that when the Old Age Pensions Act was being considered we had discussed the question of a contributory system, and had further considered compulsory contributions. I said I had instructed that the figures be gathered together in order that I might be informed as to the situation. I said this without in any sense indicating that it could be treated as a policy. My mind was running along the idea of some system in a new country like this being entered upon that would not leave, as some of the older countries have found, a very large number of old and dependent people to be provided for, but that beginning in their youthful years, as soon as they were able to earn their living, by making contributions, large or small, there would be accumulated a fund that would ensure them from want in their old age. That is a very different thing from enunciating a policy, which I have not done, and which I would not do on the committee stage of a resolution dealing with an increase of the federal contribution from fifty per cent to seventy-five per cent; I do not think I would choose that as the occasion for a declaration of policy on a matter of this kind. I merely indicated it to the committee in order that its members might consider the problem, because they have given a great deal of attention to it. For instance, the right hon. gentleman opposite (Mr. Mackenzie King) has, the former Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) has, and the former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has, and as well the member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) and the member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps). I merely mentioned these matters because it occurred to me that it is desirable that such matters affecting the welfare of this country should be thought of from time to time, regardless of our party affiliations, and I was merely making the suggestion that this was worthy of their consideration. In fact my mind is free to arrive at any conclusion that after mature consideration I think may be best for the country as a whole.

.... equal to one-half of the net sum paid out during the preceding quarter by such province for pensions, pursuant to a provincial statute authorizing and providing for the payment of such pensions to the persons and under the conditions specified in this act and the regulations made hereunder.

As far as the blind are concerned I think there is a universal feeling that if the provinces treated them as being eligible for pension before the age of seventy and asked for cooperative action on the .part of the Dominion, such action would be taken, but no province has made that request or taken the initial step of providing for such pensions, although there lies the liability.

I should like to say a word on this question, because I think it is one of those humanitarian matters which should be entirely taken out of politics. The care of the helpless, the infirm, the aged and the blind should be a matter apart from our party' discussions. As has been stated by the exMinister of Justice, the province of Quebec occupies a very unfortunate position at present-in this respect. Owing to our peculiar social system we have a large number of institutions in almost every constituency which are able to look after the aged people in many cases better than they could look after themselves. Prime Minister says, that the basis of this measure is a provincial statute, but we brought about that condition when we ourselves adopted a statute which provided that when the provincial statute was adopted the Dominion would act.
I have no doubt that if the finances of Canada permitted them to do so, the Prime Minister and his colleagues would have granted 100 per cent instead of 75 per cent; that is just one step further. "I think our present system is very faulty; I frequently receive letters from old people in my constituency asking for this old age pension, and I have to refer them to the provincial government, with the result that very little satisfaction is obtained. I support the bill, because I think any further step in the way of helping unfortunate people, especially in the eastern provinces where conditions are different from those in the western provinces, deserves support. Our younger ipeople go west, those who have not gone to the United States, and the old people stay at home; that is the condition in the three maritime provinces and in Quebec. I think under the circumstances this government should go one step further and try to bring about an arrangement under which the Dominion would come to the assistance of the poor people and of the blind as well. I should just like to say this in answer to the leader of the opposition: In 1927 there was at Winnipeg the most representative political convention that has ever been held in this country. There were present men of business, professional men, representatives of every walk in life, of every human activity, so far as Canada was concerned. At that convention the Conservative party determined that old age pensions should be a federal undertaking and they made that a plank in their platform. The same convention which passed those resolutions honoured me by selecting me as the leader of their party, and to the best of my ability I presented to the Canadian people the policy of the party as outlined at that convention. I purpose referring briefly to the speech from which he quoted in order to indicate the stand I then took; and then I shall make one or two further observations. In 1926 there took place in this house a debate, from which the hon. gentleman quoted, on a resolution similar to the one now before us. In the course of my remarks at that time I directed attention to a report of a committee of this house on the subject in 1924. The terms of that committee's recommendation were stated in these words:
Your committee further recommends that the government communicate with the various provincial governments to ascertain if they are disposed to adopt the above system and enact the necessary legislation.
We were urging the government of the day to do this and to bring in legislation acceptable to all the provinces. I pause to make this point. The burden of our objection was that the legislation then introduced and subsequently put into effect, having been in force up to the present time, would not be acceptable to all the provinces. The proof of the soundness of that stand is the fact that only a certain number of the provinces have been able to take advantage of that legislation. Up to this time several provinces have not availed themselves of it. Some declare they cannot take advantage of it, and yet they are paying their share to the participation of other provinces in the benefits of the legislation.
The situation is quite clear. In the west there is a preponderating element of younger persons; in the extreme east you have exactly the reverse. The smaller maritime provinces, we pointed out, would be burdened with a charge which it was absolutely impossible for them to bear, whereas in the west the burden was very much lightened by the large number of younger people living there in comparison with the aged. It was on that ground that we combated, not the principle of the legislation but the wisdom of its form; and if ever a party was justified in any stand
it has taken, this party has been vindicated over and over again in its attitude towards that legislation by the fact that the legislation has not been and cannot be adopted b}r all the provinces of Canada.
On that occasion I made this statement:
I supported the principle, and have done so for years. I did so long before this government had the courage to bring it in-
I was referring to the government of the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), and I made that statement because I thought the principle was good. I took that stand then, and for several years prior to that, from my place in the house, I had urged some measure of old age pensions. Yet my hon. friend has the audacity to-night to say that we of the Conservative party consistently opposed this measure of relief to the aged of the country. I then referred to what action the Senate might take. My hon. friend suggested that we rather wished that the Senate would throw it out. On that occasion 1 said:
So far as I am concerned, if I had any influence with the Senate I would advise them to pass the legislation, even though it is of an abortive character, so that the uselessness of it may recoil upon the government's head.
Again, I say, the ineffectiveness and injustice of that legislation have been amply demonstrated in the efforts of the last few years to put it into operation. I am not going to quote further because it is not neoessary for the point I wish to make.
Let me say a few words on the principle of the legislation. Ten years ago, long before my hon. friend came to the house, and for several years prior to the placing of the present legislation on the statute books, I took the stand, as I take it now, that a proper system of old age pensions should be a contributory system. But we always contended that certain other measures should be adopted to take care of the aged who were on our hands and who, of course, could not participate in a contributory system. The government of my hon. friends opposite, under the right hon. gentleman who is now leader of the opposition, made no attempt whatever to work out a contributory system-not the slightest attempt. They made no effort to introduce a permanent and definite system of old age pensions. They did introduce a system which, as I have already said, has been taken advantage of by a few provinces but not by all.
Then there is the second point: we contended that the system should be federal; that is to say, that it should be a measure
