Mr. Chairman, if my remarks at this time were likely to cause further controversy I should hesitate to make them. I feel, however, that they may tend to remove what misunderstanding there may have been concerning my statements in the maritime provinces.
Just before six o'clock the Prime Minister referred to statements I had made when speaking in Prince Edward Island, which he spoke of as a Liberal province, and then proceeded to compare those remarks with my statements in Nova Scotia, which was spoken of as a Conservative province. I gathered that the comments by my right hon. friend were based on a speech made in the course of the debate on the budget a few days ago by the present Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Rhodes), who I am glad to see in his seat at the moment. On that occasion the minister said he had heard my statements over the radio and for that reason he was quite sure he was giving a correct report of my remarks. May I say to him that his statement as to what he heard over the radio was right. I contend, however, that the inference he sought to convey was wrong. The statement made is that while in Charlottetown I said I was not averse to a 100 per cent old age pension scheme but that I thought in the first place there should be an accounting with the provinces so that we might learn the respective obligations of the federal and provincial authorities. According to my hon. friend that was the statement I made in Prince Edward Island and I now state that he has correctly repeated what he heard.
The Prime Minister sought to leave the impression that my statement was intended to win votes in the smallest eastern province, that it was an appeal to that province to support a 100 per cent old age pension scheme. On the other hand in Nova Scotia it is alleged I put matters in such a way that the Liberal party might, through a different representation, gain at the expense of the Conservative party. I made, to all intent and purposes, the same statements in Prince Edward Island with respect to old age pensions that I made in Nova Scotia, and in all other provinces in which I spoke on the subject.
Old Age Pensions Act

I have before me a report of my speech in Prince Edward Island as it appears in the Charlottetown Guardian of June 23, 1930. Apparently my^words were taken down by a shorthand reporter, and I ask the committee, when listening to my words, to judge whether my statements were calculated to win votes by promises in connection with old age pensions. I shall now read the report of my speech because it emphasizes the point I have been trying to make concerning provincial grants. From the point of view of winning support I admit the criticizing of the giving of provincial grants is not popular, but I do believe that careful consideration of the view I have expressed is essential to save our country from a very serious condition with respect to future taxation, something to which we ought now to be giving much more attention than we really are. Of my speech delivered on June 22 in Charlottetown, the report in the Charlottetown Guardian of June 23, 1930, is as follows:
May I say this, I am not averse to the idea of taking over the old age pensions law as federal obligation, but I think before we take over any more obligations at the present time, we had better have a pretty careful accounting of what the total amounts are of those things that we are contributing to, and what the total expenditures are, both provincially and federally. This is all bound up with the constitution of our country. When the provinces came into confederation they gave up certain rights of taxation. For that they were given in consideration; they were given an agreement to get so much in the way of subsidy. That means that they would be handed out of the federal treasury certain grants of money which the federal government would have to raise in the form of taxes. Under that arrangement Prince Edward Island got so much. The intention of confederation was that each of us-the provinces and the Dominion-would work in our own fields. Now I think the time has come when those arrangements, especially with regard to subsidy should be revised even more _ than they have been. When we had a Dominion-provincial conference at Ottawa, I found that the premiers of the different provinces and their ministers all took the view that whatever is being given to them from the federal treasury should be given in a lump sum and that the provinces be allowed to spend that money as they think best. They stated in so many words: We don't like this contribution for highways, etc. Give us the money and let us do what we think best! I think that is a fair way to go on. Let us make the subsidies fair and let each province expend the money as it thinks advisable.
I am quite prepared at the appropriate time to go very carefully into this whole question of the matter of subsidy and what should be given, and if in this connection it may seem advisable for the Dominion government to take over the old age pensions we can get our British North America Act amended to take over that particular charge, and we can write off against that expenditure what we propose to give in
IMr. Mackenzie King.]
the way of subsidy. But a matter of this kind that relates to the Dominion as a whole, in relation to the several provinces should not be made a matter of party polities, but should be made a matter of straight business and good government.
That was the statement I made in the maritime provinces and which I made repeatedly in this house during the last parliament. I have made a similar statement frequently this session and it is one I should like to repeat at this moment.
I do submit that however well intentioned the Prime Minister may be when he makes additional grants for old age pensions, when he proposes additional grants for technical education and binds future governments for fifteen years by a bill now .before the house, when he pledges further grants of very considerable amounts for unemployment, when he proposes to make a grant running into many millions of dollars to meet a great emergency existing in another part of the country-I say that when my hon. friends consider that they have had at this session so considerally to increase taxation, when they know that at the close of the fiscal year they will be far behind in revenues and will have enormous deficits and that there will be necessity for imposing additional taxation, they ought to be giving more in the way of thought to the additional burdens of taxation they are loading on the backs of the people.

Some have been discontinued, but on the other hand there will be an increase of publicity within Canada. That is following the plan that was adopted by the government last fall to try out something that I think has not been given a trial, namely colonization at home. We have plenty of people to work on who have come into the country in the last few years, ostensibly to go on the land, but who have drifted into industry. Now they are finding themselves cast adrift from industry and the effort of the government is to give those people who can carry on farming operations in such a way as to sustain themselves an opportunity, at the least possible expense to the government, to go on the land. Any publicity this year and possibly next year will be confined to such as is necessary within Canada itself, in the hope that that effort will contribute to relieving distress in industrial and mining sections. No publicity of a major kind will be carried on in Great Britain, and none at all in Europe. By that I mean the kind of publicity that is calculated to bring into Canada at the present time people who are not equipped to take care of themselves financially and otherwise. We cannot, of course, dissociate ourselves entirely from contact with Great Britain with respect to the migration of people, but the British government and the Overseas Settlement Department know very well-we have had many communications on the subject with them-that the time is not opportune to encourage any considerable movement of people. Information was given some weeks ago-I am speaking from memory -as to a plan which had been worked out between the two great railway companies and the head of the department to place people on the land in order to relieve the unemployment situation. I think it was stated that some thousands of single men and over one thousand families had been placed in that way and that the movement had been quite successful in that a very small percentage of the men had gone back to the cities. I would ask the minister just what was the basis of that plan. Were families placed on the farms with the object of purchasing them eventually, or were they simply placed on abandoned farms to relieve them for the time being, perhaps with a garden or something of that sort to help them carry along?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The operation of the plan commenced last fall, after several interviews with the colonization departments of the railways and after it had been approved by the presidents of the two roads. It was generally agreed between the government and the railways that the combined colonization effort should be directed first towards taking desirable single men out of the ranks of the unemployed and placing them with farmers who could give them work and probably some pay. Well qualified men, of course, got more pay than those less qualified. Instructions were given by the railways to their agents to survey the various districts throughout Canada and ascertain the number of men the farmers could absorb, and the same instructions were given to the land settlement branch and the field supervisors of the soldier settlement board. They were instructed to survey the situation with care so that men who were taken from the ranks of the unemployed would be of a type likely to give satisfaction to the farmers who employed them. That plan is now being worked out; it is being pressed with a good deal of vigour, and it is meeting, I think, with a very large measure of success. The figures are returned to me monthly. I have not under my hand the latest figures, but if I remember aright somewhere in the neighbourhood of ten thousand single men have been placed on the farms with farmers. I was rather surprised to note how many farmers like to have a good hired man around the place. It was extremely encouraging from our standpoint to find that there were quite a large number of farmers in Canada who were doing pretty well. They are absorbing a great
number of the unemployed and this, remember, without any extra cost to the government, for we are using the same staff which heretofore had been engaged in outside immigration work taking care of the men coming into this country.
With respect to the families, this picture presented itself to the railways and to myself. There were many families who, during the last few years, attracted no doubt by the apparently prosperous position of industry, had come into the industrial centres seeking jobs in industry. They had accumulated some hundreds, and in some cases some thousands of dollars, and then they found themselves out of work, with their savings gradually dwindling for rent and taxes. We found a desire among them to go back to the land if they could get a farm suited to their purpose and within their means. We have found that many families, just such as I have described, are very anxious to go back to the land and to be sure at least that they have something to support them. The last figure I got as to the number of families placed upon the land in that way-I am speaking from memory-was in the neighbourhood of 2,700. I intend, in conjunction with the railways-and I hope as time goe3 on to be able to enlist other organizations which heretofore have been engaged solely in bringing people outside of Canada into this country-to concentrate our efforts in a way best calculated to ensure success in that work until the time shall have arrived, and I hope it will not be so very long, when Canada will be able to take a more comprehensive view of inducing people to come here. But when they do come, it will be my effort to see that they come under some disciplined plan so that there will be the least possible number of failures.
Is it hoped that these family settlements will be permanent, that they will purchase farms?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Yes.
Are these abandoned farms held by the soldier settlement board, or by the railways, or by both?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Both.

I notice an item for loans to boys. Is there anything being done in that respect now? Is free passage still being given to boys, and are many taking advantage of it?
Supply-Immigration

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
We are not carrying on that work now.
Mr. (LUCAS: Do I understand the minister to say that free pasage is not being given to boys of from 14 to 19 years of age, from the old land at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: None now. Some boys were coming out to the provinces under agreement with us, but they have already arrived, and no more boys are being brought out.
When was that discontinued?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Some of the provinces discontinued it at the beginning of last year. Others brought out a few this year-Ontario, for instance. Saskatchewan brought out about forty, and Nova Scotia about fifty.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
No; that matter was
brought to my attention some time ago and in communication with the railways I learned that such advertising had been discontinued. Boys coming out under various schemes by agreement with the provinces have already arrived, and no more are coming.

When were such advertisements discontinued? Only last week I received a letter from the old country informing me that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is still advertising for people to come out to go on farms in the maritime provinces

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The hon. member is not referring to boys?

No.
[Mr. Speakman.l

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Nova Scotia and New
Brunswick, so far as I know, have always maintained that they could take care of selected families. Nova Scotia asked for one hundred families, and New Brunswick for a similar number. Requests were made particularly for British and Scandinavian races. We agreed to admit that number of people, and I believe it was stipulated that each family must have $1,000. Undoubtedly the railroads knew about the coming of those families, and the fact that they were keen for business accounts for the advertisements. I expect however that this year only about one-quarter the number will come out to the maritime provinces.
Mr. LUCAS Does the minister think it advisable under present conditions to spend large sums of money in repatriation work?
Mr. GORDON The only money spent at the present time for repatriation is $50,000 to the province of Quebec, and that province is spending an equal amount. While it may seem rather paradoxical to spend money on repatriation at this time, I think there is justification for it. We ought to be pleased to know that a large number of Canadians are returning. Although in the past we had hoped for their return we did not expect that it would be for the reasons which prompt some of them to come. Under any circumstances, however, they are welcome.
Surely we should not have to pay for their coming.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: That may be the view of the hon. member, but I am inclined to think that this money is being very well spent by the province of Quebec, and I should be reluctant to see such expenditures disturbed.
I wonder if that statement applies to the repatriation of orientals in British Columbia? Would the minister spend $50,000 for the repatriation of orientals from British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Where to?
To the orient.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I think the hon. member has his gears in reverse, has he not?

No, it would be highly desirable to repatriate them to the orient on the condition that they stayed away.
In vote No. 124 there is provision "for loans for stock, equipment, etc., for Canadians boys." I have always been in favour of such loans rather than bringing people from overseas. Do

Supply-I mmigra tion
those boys have to have money to begin with? Are they given land, or what are the general conditions?
While the minister is getting that information I might save time by asking another simple question. Under an order in council regarding immigration there is a clause that Americans may come in provided they have sufficient funds to maintain them until they secure work, or words to that effect. I should like to have an idea from the minister as to what sum might reasonably be expected to keep such an immigrant until he obtained work, especially under present conditions when work is very much at a premium. A man out of work at present may be in a similar position twelve months from now, and under such circumstances I am wondering what sum might be considered sufficient.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: There is no fixed sum.

How is it arrived at? The
order in council says that such men shall have sufficient money to keep them until they get work. Is it possible to tell by looking at a man, by knowing his name or by any other external evidence when he may expect work?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Such decisions are left to the judgment of the officers at the ports of entry. They have to size up the men and make decisions. Some men may have $10,000 in their pockets and I might refuse to let them in; other men may have only 50 cents and might be allowed in. A great deal depends on the judgment of the officers at the border ports of entry.

Such practice is not without
some merit. We all know that a man's character is his best asset. At the same time, however, to tell all subordinate officers simply to use their judgment is not a good system. An officer may say, "Oh yes, come in" to almost any person. In these days when we are asked to pay large sums to relieve unemployment we Should have a most definite plan. Such men ought at least to have $200 in their pockets.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
They have to have more
than that.

A minute ago the minister
said only 50 cents might be required.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
A man would not be
allowed to come in here with any amount of money and simply look around until he secured work we are trying to provide for our own people. He would have to assure the officer at the port of entry that he had means sufficient to provide for himself for
some time. I have taken the stand that a man should have funds sufficient to carry him over the next winter. That attitude has been passed on to the officers at the ports of entry and has been adopted as a principle. The officers are instructed always to use their own judgment, leaning slightly towards rigidity in the enforcement of the law.

Those are the instructions
sent out, are they?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Yes, instructions very
much along that line.
I think those instructions are enforced on the other side of the line and not when the immigrant gets to Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Yes.

Reverting to the matter of the families who at the present time are going on land, some of whom are purchasing land in the hands of the soldier settlement board, may I ask upon what principle the price of that land is based? Is it based upon the amount against a particular farm, or is the land appraised quite regardless of any debts which may have been accumulated against it by its former occupant?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will
let the matter stand until we come to the soldier and general land settlement votes I shall be pleased to answer him.
Very well.

Have you any information
about the Canadian boys?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
There is about $30,000 in
that item but we do not anticipate we will spend any of it this year.
You are not encouraging the Canadian boys to go on the land any more!

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The provinces at the conference did not care to join with us in that effort this year; therefore we are advancing no money.

Why the vote if you are
not going to spend it? I do not think it could be better spent than in encouraging our own boys to go on the land.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
We are not advancing the money this year because we are directing our whole effort in another direction, that is, to getting people who are able to go on the land themselves with their families without expense to the government. I am of opinion that a halt must be made on advances by this government to people to go on the land until at
Supply-Immigration

[east I have had a further opportunity of considering the policy. Sometimes I doubt the wisdom of making advances to put people on the land, because in my judgment at least it has not been a very great success.

That is a matter of policy
for consideration by the minister. If he is not going to spend the money why put it in the estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
It is a small amount. Item agreed to.
Empire settlement scheme, including grants to immigration societies, provinces, women's hostels, etc., as may be authorized by the governor general in council, $200,000.
What is the difference between the women's hostels mentioned in this item and the women's hostels mentioned in the preceding item? There seems to be a duplication of phraseology, if not of activity.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The words "women's
hostels" should not be in the previous item at all, because no grants are made to institutions of that kind. I expect the wording has been carried forward from other years. The hostels under the British empire settlement agreement do get some grants.

What societies are getting
assistance under this vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: None; but the grants will be continued to the women's hostels.
They will not get the $200,000, will they?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: That is the total amount
It seems to me we are passing these votes just because they were passed last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: There is a reduction of
Yes, but we have discontinued the empire settlement scheme, yet we are continuing the grants. The empire settlement scheme is at an end, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: No.

Are people still coming out
under it?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
There are a few people
coming out.
In New Brunswick there are some.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.
That is where the provinces take care of it, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The empire settlement
takes care of it under the agreement.

I think if that vote were
cut in half the minister would have sufficient so far as he can explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
We will not spend that
amount.

Then why vote it? Just
because it has always been voted?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
No. At the time these
estimates were made up we reduced the amount by $350,000, and it was anticipated that it would be spent this year. It is quite true that we will not spend this amount, but nobody will be hurt by the passing of the item so far as I can see.

May I take the opportunity of bringing to the attention of the minister the unsatisfactory condition of the empire settlers in western Canada. Frequently we make a reduction of the indebtedness of our soldier settlers to the extent of 30 per cent of their land and equipment. If you make inquiry among the empire settlers you will find that usually they have paid for their land a price equal to the price paid by the original settler. The situation is simply this, -under present conditions the empire settlers carrying that load of liability find it impossible to succeed. I suggest to the minister that he take into consideration in cases where the prices paid were excessive the question of reducing those prices.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The situation of the empire settlers in western Canada-that is the three thousand family scheme?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: That has given me a great deal of concern. There is no doubt those men bought land at prices very much higher than they are to-day, and having regard to the setback in connection with the crop failures, it is obvious that many of them are not only unable to pay their instalments, but are having great difficulty in holding their farms. I do not propose to see any of those men have their contracts rescinded. The whole situation in respect to those settlers is under consideration, and I hope some equitable adjustment may be arrived at, although it is going to be very difficult because so many other people are in the same position with the mortgage and trust companies.

In view of the fact
that this service is to be reorganized and that the cost of administration will be reduced, would the minister explain the decrease in this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
There is a total decrease
of $657,000, with an increase on the other side of the ledger of $302,000 leaving a general decrease of $355,000. That is purely a change of bookkeeping. Farms which were administered formerly under the general land settlement vote now will be administered under the soldier land settlement vote, which shows an apparent increase of $302,000 for that reason. On the other hand, the administration of general land settlement is decreased by $657,000, showing a net decrease of $355,000 for the year.
Could the minister tell me in a general way how the price now arrived at compares with the price for which the land was sold originally?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I imagine a great deal
would depend upon the year in which it was sold. I think it would be a fair statement to say that to-day valuations are considerably decreased from the original price; there will be a loss in almost every case.

I agree with the minister
that it is right and proper that the land should be sold to-day at its actual value, but that puts us in this position:	What about
the empire settlers who are on the land; can you justly refuse them a revaluation? You cannot put yourself in the position of forcing off these men and then selling the land to someone else at a much lower price. If you are willing to take your loss, as you must, and sell to the newcomer at 50 per cent less than the other man paid, why not do justice and keep the empire settler on the land and give him a rebate?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: It does seem an anomaly.
You cannot get out of that position once you do the proper thing and sell the land at its present value; why should you turn off the man originally put there?

I think something will have to be done with regard to the British empire settlers. As I understand it, most of these men were settled on abandoned soldier settlement land without a reduction. The soldier settlers proper were granted a reduction of 30 per cent last year, and some of these people coming out at the present time are being placed on these lands at their present value. Under present conditions it is hopeless to expect these empire settlers to pay for their lands at the prices for which they were sold a few years ago, and in order to keep them on the land some revaluation will have to be made. I trust that the minister will give this matter his very serious consideration. I have had a number of representations made to me by these men, and I promised to bring the matter to the attention of the minister. Then there is another point with regard to which I should like to ask a question. I refer to what is known as the tripartite agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The New Brunswick
agreement?

No, it applies in the west.
Here is the situation; A soldier settler takes over land from another soldier settler; that transfer is endorsed by the board, but since the second man was not originally a bona-fide soldier settler, to-day he does not get that 30 per cent reduction. I have in mind the case of a soldier settler who was settled in 1921 by the board. Later on, because of ill health, he was advised to give up farming, so he sold his farm to another soldier settler. After being away for a couple of years he
Supply-Labour

came back again and repurchased the land. Now he is refused the 30 per cent reduction, whereas had he remained on the land continually he would have been entitled to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
That would require a
change in the statute.

I understand so, but I
should like to ask the minister to give this matter his careful consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I am aware of some
cases such as the hon. member has described. There is an apparent hardship, and I have the matter under consideration to see if some method cannot be evolved which will overcome that hardship. Fortunately there are not many of those cases.

As a matter of fact,
Mr. Chairman, both when the revaluation was permitted and the 30 per cent reduction was granted it was in the mind of the committee that those genuine eases of tripartite agreements were covered by the act. That was the intention of the committee, but it turns out that according to the phraseology of the act they are not covered.
Then I should like to say just one word in support of what has been said already as to the position of empire settlers and other civilian purchasers of soldier settlement lands. I am not going to bring forward any individual cases, because I think that is more or less a waste of time since they cannot be considered at a time like this. But I have a case in mind which is typical of a great many cases. It is the case of a man who moved from the dry area of southern Alberta into my riding in central Alberta, and who purchased an abandoned farm through the board. Up to about 1930 he did keep up his payments, but of course he is utterly unable to do so this year. I appreciate, and most of the settlers are begininng to appreciate, the fact that the minister has no intention of either putting them off the land or permitting them to be forced off at the present time. Naturally however, their debt is accumulating, the arrears becoming quite a burden; and while they are confident that the minister intends to safeguard them at the moment, they are looking to the future without much hope. The suggestion made by a number of them was that during this year, at least at a time when they do not expect payments to be made on a number of these farms, current interest be cancelled so that their arrears may not increase to a hopeless point. I realize that the minister has just taken charge of his department and is now reorganizing it, but I have no doubt he has the whole

situation in mind. As regards these empire settlers; the soldiers who became settlers, not having been originally soldier settlers; and those civilians who purchased land abandoned by soldiers, none of whom have received the benefit of the reduction, I hope their cases will all be taken into the minister's careful consideration at his leisure, when he is relieved of his responsibilities in connection with the Beauharnois committee. I should like to see something done for these people, not merely from motives of generosity but on a business basis, so that they may be able to pay for the land and retain their self respect.
Perhaps the minister will make a statement in regard to the Burch case which I have discussed with him privately several times. Is he still prepared to give consideration to this case?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: It is the ease of the carpenter; I know it very well. I may tell my hon. friend frankly that I have been struggling with the case, because while there is a good deal of equity on the side of the claimant, there is so little that I can do. However, I have it still under review and I hope to find some means whereby he can be compensated legally.

I am glad to hear the minister say that, because the soldier settlement board has certainly benefited to a considerable extent through this man. He is a carpenter, and returned soldier, and when so much has been done for others I think his case should be given consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: It is a meritorious case.
